text.p: The United States, ending months of growing criticism of its wait-and-see stance, is again plunging into Middle East diplomacy with vigour as the stakes get higher and prospects more bleak.

In her first major speech on the Arab-Israeli peace process, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday announced her intention to make her maiden trip to the region late this month provided there is "some progress" on the issue of security in the area.
And in a shift of U.S. policy, she said she would press Israel and the Palestinians to negotiate much more quickly than originally planned on a final peace settlement.
The Clinton administration -- and Albright in particular -- has had a pretty good foreign policy run in the seven months since she took office, emerging as the "star" of the Cabinet.

It saw the enlargement of NATO, crafted a new NATO-Russia security relationship, won Senate approval of the Chemical Weapons Convention, persuaded Congress to raise foreign affairs funding and improved ties with China among other things.

But last week's suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market refocused attention on the intractable Middle East, worsening an already severe "crisis of confidence" between Israelis and Palestinians and striking a new blow at a crumbling peace process launched under U.S. leadership in 1991.

It is Albright's first real foreign policy crisis, a test of her ability as America's top diplomat. Analysts and U.S. officials give her high marks for style and communicating with the public but some still wonder about her ability to shape the substance of policy.
Her predecessor, Warren Christopher, made Mideast peace his primary pursuit during President Bill Clinton's first term.
But analysts felt Christopher's decision to take dozens of trips there, compared to two to China, reflected skewed U.S. interests and squandered the secretary of state's clout.
Albright long resisted repeated calls to make a Mideast trip -- travel that many view as a key manifestation of direct high-level U.S. involvement in the peace process.
She insisted she was active in keeping Israeli-Palestinian talks in motion through telephone calls and talks with the full array of Mideast leaders who visited Washington.

The plan was to hold her trip in reserve until she could achieve something significant by journeying to the region. But some analysts speculated she also feared being drawn into a diplomatic morass with no easy solution.
Her sensitivity on the subject erupted after the bombing last week, when first Clinton and then Albright was asked if the attack would force her to get personally involved.
"Let me make this clear: I am directly involved in this," she snapped as she spoke to reporters on a flight from Asia.
Two days later, aides contacted the National Press Club about arrangements for Albright to deliver Wednesday's speech.

More clearly than ever, Albright, in her speech, and Clinton, at a White House news conference, made plain that the United States does not feel Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has made a 100 percent effort to fight terrorism.

According to Robert Satloff of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, the leaders sided significantly with Israel when they insisted security is the "primary focus" and must be dealt with first, before peace talks can resume.

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross will discuss these issues on a trip to the region this weekend. But U.S. officials said Arafat need only take "minimum steps" on ensuring Israel's security for Albright to proceed with her trip plans.
Clinton, along with Albright, also criticised Israel for taking unilateral steps, including building Jewish settlements on traditionally Arab land, that enraged the Palestinians.

Washington had been considering endorsing accelerated talks on a final Israel-Palestinian peace settlement. It decided to do so after it concluded the gradual approach of the Oslo peace accords, designed to build confidence as the two sides resolved lesser issues, was not working.

Final status talks are meant to settle the borders and nature of the Palestinian entity -- Palestinians want an independent state -- and the administration of Jerusalem. Albright will pursue this on her Mideast trip.
